stories.headline: Update: Iran Says US Struck Qeshm Island in New Exchange of Strikes
stories.summary:
The United States struck several locations on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Persian Gulf, Iran's semi-official Mehr News Agency reported on Tuesday. The two sides appeared to be intensifying attacks in their ongoing war, according to Bloomberg's account of the report.

Qeshm is the largest island in the Persian Gulf and sits in the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's most important shipping routes. The reported strikes add a new geographic target to a conflict that has previously involved strikes on Bahrain and the arrival of a third US carrier group in the Middle East. The details of what was hit, and any casualties or damage, were not immediately available.

The report had not been independently confirmed by US officials at the time of publication, and Washington's account of the strikes was not included in the initial coverage. The new exchange comes as the conflict continues to draw in regional states and raises concerns about shipping and energy supplies through the Gulf. Further US and Iranian statements are expected in the coming hours.

stories.headline: Update: US Confirms Criminal Probe of Nvidia Partner Megaspeed Over Chip Exports
stories.summary:
The US Departments of Justice and Commerce confirmed in a joint statement on Monday that they have been investigating Singapore-based Megaspeed since 2024 for potential export control violations. The company is suspected of helping ship Nvidia's advanced chips to China. The agencies said it was "in the public interest to provide the facts and address inaccurate information" about the case.

The statement laid out a timeline. Commerce investigators requested records from Nvidia about sales to Megaspeed in May 2025, and Nvidia placed the company on its no-sell list in June 2025. Agents then conducted an on-site check in Singapore with local law enforcement and interviewed Alice Huang, then Megaspeed's chief executive. The Justice Department subsequently took the lead in a criminal investigation. Megaspeed is the largest buyer of Nvidia chips in Southeast Asia and said on Sunday it had launched an internal probe.

The disclosure follows the resignation last week of Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang after revelations of extramarital affairs, one allegedly with Alice Huang, whom US authorities suspect of spying for Beijing. China denies the allegation. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has blamed Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick's department for weak oversight of chip exports, and Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month. Jensen Huang has agreed to testify in Congress, including before the House Select Committee on China. The White House said Monday it would further restrict China's access to AI chips from firms such as Nvidia.

stories.headline: Jeffries to Force Tallied Caucus Vote on Speaker Nomination
stories.summary:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries plans to require House Democrats to take a tallied vote this week on whether to nominate him for speaker, according to two sources cited by Axios. His allies had previously hoped to nominate him by acclamation, so the move marks a shift in tactics.

The recorded vote would show whether Jeffries has the support to become speaker when the new Congress convenes on Jan. 3. Axios reported that if he loses more than 40 votes, he could be in trouble, while a smaller defection would likely allow him to sail through. Democrats are preparing to take control of the House after the midterm elections.

Jeffries is expected to be re-elected as Democratic leader following a period of successful fundraising and caucus unity during the second Trump administration. The result of the internal vote will be an early indicator of how unified the incoming majority is as it prepares to confront the White House on issues including taxes and subpoenas.

stories.headline: Trump Says Alaska Voters Picked 'Wrong' Sullivan; Data Shows Peltola Lead Holds
stories.summary:
Almost two weeks after the midterms, Alaska's Senate race remains the last without a projected winner. With 98 percent of votes counted, Democrat Mary Peltola leads Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, who has held the seat since 2015 and is seeking a third term.

The ballot also listed a second candidate, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., a retired school teacher. Republicans argued the similar names confused voters and brought an unsuccessful legal challenge. President Trump has posted repeatedly that the race was "rigged" and that votes for "the fake Dan Sullivan" were meant for the incumbent. A New York Times report before the election alleged that Democratic operatives linked to the Peltola campaign tried to recruit spoiler candidates. Peltola denies knowledge of any such scheme, and Sullivan Jr. denies ties to her campaign. Election law expert Joshua Douglas noted that recruiting candidates is not illegal.

BBC Verify's analysis found that even combining both Sullivans' votes would not overcome Peltola's lead. In Alaska's ranked-choice system, over a third of Sullivan Jr.'s first-choice voters left their second choice blank, and Peltola received nearly twice as many of the remaining second-choice votes as the incumbent. The BBC said this undercuts claims of widespread confusion among Republican voters. The final result will help determine the Senate's partisan balance.

stories.headline: Palestinian Woman, 72, Shot Dead in West Bank Village Where Israeli Settlers Recently Moved In
stories.summary:
A 72-year-old Palestinian woman, Fadwa al-Fahidat, was shot dead Monday evening in the village of al-Duyuk al-Tahta near Jericho, the Palestinian health ministry said. Doctors at a Jericho hospital said she was shot in the head, and several other Palestinians and Israelis were wounded. The village is in an area meant to be under full Palestinian Authority control, though Israel retains security control over the properties where settlers recently settled.

Accounts of the incident conflict. Palestinian reports say she was shot outside her home, and that her son raced to the scene, collided with an empty Israeli vehicle parked outside the family home and injured settlers standing nearby, after which settlers opened fire. The Israel Defense Forces said "terrorists" rammed an Israeli vehicle, left their car with weapons and attacked the occupants, and that Israelis fired after rocks were thrown. The IDF statement did not mention the woman's death and said security forces were pursuing suspects.

Tensions have been high since settlers moved into eight purchased houses in the village on 4 November in what they described as a secretive operation. The Israeli rights group B'Tselem describes a prolonged campaign of settler attacks, intimidation and land seizures there, with troops now stationed nearby to protect the new settlement. In a separate Monday incident, eight Palestinians were injured near Tuqu, south of Bethlehem, when hit by a vehicle driven by an Israeli settler; the IDF called it a traffic accident, while the Palestinian foreign ministry called it a terrorist attack.

Also Monday, Israel's Civil Administration announced the allocation of more than 28 square km of land in the northern Jordan Valley. All settlements are considered illegal under international law, a position Israel disputes.

stories.headline: Democrats Weigh Tax Increases as They Prepare to Take Control of Congress
stories.summary:
Congressional Democrats, having won control of Congress in the midterms, are discussing options for raising taxes to pay for their priorities, according to coverage from Axios, Fox News, National Review and the New York Times. Their wish list includes expanding Medicare, reversing recently enacted spending cuts and restoring subsidies for Affordable Care Act exchange plans. The national debt currently stands at about $40.6 trillion.

Republican-leaning commentators argue the shift contradicts campaign messaging. National Review's Jim Geraghty wrote that Democrats ran on restoring affordability and are now focusing on tax increases, though he noted a small victory in Democrats acknowledging the deficit and debt exist. He pointed out that only a handful of candidates, mostly in deep-blue areas, discussed taxing the rich during the campaign; Michigan's Abdul El-Sayed backed higher marginal rates on earnings over $1 million and a wealth tax on billionaires.

Democrats have generally argued that higher taxes on top earners and large wealth holdings are a fair way to fund health care and social programs while addressing deficits. The top individual rate currently applies above $640,601 for individuals and $768,701 for married couples. Any tax legislation would still need to pass the Senate and avoid a presidential veto, and the new Congress is not seated until January, so concrete proposals remain at an early stage.

stories.headline: Update: Nvidia Reports Earnings in First Quarter After Jensen Huang's Resignation
stories.summary:
Nvidia is set to release third-quarter results after the close of trading Tuesday, its first earnings report since founder Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive last week. Investors and analysts will be listening for hints about near-term changes at the company, and about any government actions the company expects, following the circumstances that led to his departure.

Huang's exit followed reports of a relationship with a Singaporean vendor, Alice Huang, who is suspected of acting as an intermediary to help China gain access to advanced chips restricted by U.S. export law. The company has said it launched an internal review. Huang had long opposed restrictions on advanced chip sales to China, arguing that selling U.S. technology encourages Chinese reliance on American products. Critics, including conservative commentators, have questioned whether Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick will face scrutiny over the episode.

The results matter beyond one company: Nvidia makes the most sought-after AI processors, and its guidance is a bellwether for the broader AI investment boom. Wall Street is watching for signals on succession, export-control compliance and demand. Incoming Democratic committee chairs have also signaled interest in oversight of the matter after they take control of Congress in January.

stories.headline: Mozambique Opposition Leader Venancio Mondlane Goes on Trial Over 2024 Election Unrest
stories.summary:
Opposition leader Venancio Mondlane went on trial Tuesday at the Supreme Court in Maputo over the deadly protests that followed Mozambique's disputed October 2024 elections. Police were heavily deployed in the capital, with authorities fearing fresh demonstrations by his supporters. Mondlane arrived early with what he called "great peace of mind" and was greeted by dozens of supporters.

He faces charges including incitement to terrorism, public instigation to commit crimes, glorifying criminal acts and incitement to collective disobedience, and could receive up to 24 years in prison if convicted of the most serious charge. Prosecutors accuse him of encouraging protests that disrupted public services, damaged property and threatened public security. Mondlane denies wrongdoing, saying he sought electoral transparency, and his party, Anamola, calls the prosecution politically motivated. The Supreme Court denies political interference.

Mondlane had challenged the declared victory of Daniel Chapo of the ruling Frelimo party, alleging widespread fraud. Amnesty International, citing civil society groups, says more than 300 people were killed in the unrest, while police put the toll at 96, including 17 officers. EU observers reported irregularities in the vote. Analysts view the trial as a major test of the country's political stability and rule of law.

stories.headline: Ukraine Strike Collapses Section of Kerch Bridge to Crimea as Russia Hits Kyiv Bridges
stories.summary:
A section of the Crimean Bridge, also known as the Kerch Bridge, collapsed on Tuesday after a Ukrainian strike. The $3.7 billion crossing, nearly 12 miles long and the longest in Europe, is a vital supply line for Russian forces and a symbolic project for President Vladimir Putin, who made its construction a priority after Russia annexed Crimea in 2014.

Ukraine's Security Service said one of the metal arches and the road span beneath it were completely destroyed, and that the railway section was preliminarily damaged. President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukrainian-made weapons were used: Palianytsia drones struck the road section, while Neptune missiles, Ruta drones and FP-5 drones hit the railway section. He described the strike as the seventh stage of a plan carried out over several weeks and as a response to Russian attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure. Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara stressed that the operation used exclusively Ukrainian weapons and technology.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov played down the damage, saying the bridge would be rebuilt "even better than before," according to Russian state media. Overnight, Moscow hit two key bridges in Kyiv, bringing much of the capital to a standstill on Tuesday.

The timing carries added weight, coming on the eve of a planned meeting in Asia between Putin, President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping, which the Kremlin has framed as a "New Yalta." The damage makes the Crimean city of Yalta effectively inaccessible from mainland Russia by the bridge until repairs are made. Ukraine has intensified attacks on Crimea over the past six months, and Russian-installed authorities imposed a state of emergency there over the summer because of power outages and fuel shortages.

stories.headline: Japan Scrambles Jets After Alleged Russian Airspace Violation Ahead of Apec Summit
stories.summary:
Japan said it launched fighter jets and lodged a strong protest after two suspected Russian aircraft violated its airspace early Tuesday off the southwestern Okinoshima island. Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara called the flight paths a "serious infringement of Japan's sovereignty" and "completely unacceptable." Moscow has not commented.

South Korea said it also deployed fighter jets after Russian military aircraft entered its air defence identification zone over the Sea of Japan, departing without violating South Korean airspace. Taiwan said its military "responded accordingly" after two Russian military aircraft entered its zone. It is unclear whether the three governments were tracking the same or different aircraft.

The last comparable incursion into Japanese airspace was in 2024, off Rebun island in Hokkaido. Tensions between Tokyo and Moscow have risen in recent months: Putin visited one of the disputed Pacific islands in August, drawing a sharp rebuke from Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, and Russia detained a Japanese journalist on spying allegations in October.

The incidents come ahead of the Apec summit in China this week, which Putin will attend alongside President Donald Trump and Xi Jinping, and are seen as a reminder of Russian military reach in the region.

stories.headline: Rep. James Comer Announces Run for Kentucky Governor
stories.summary:
Rep. James Comer, the Kentucky Republican who chairs the House Oversight Committee, announced Monday night that he is running for governor of Kentucky in 2027. He said he aims to flip the governor's mansion from Democratic to Republican control.

"Serving this state is a calling for me," Comer said while unveiling his campaign, adding that Kentucky needs a leader whose policies will lead to growth and good-paying jobs.

The announcement follows a midterm cycle in which Democrats took control of Congress and a historic number of state legislatures. Comer's bid would take him away from a committee that has been central to congressional investigations, at a time when Democratic control of the House is expected to reshape oversight priorities. Democrats currently hold the Kentucky governorship, and the race is likely to be watched as an early test of Republican strength after the midterm losses.

stories.headline: Imran Khan Appeals for Urgent Medical Care, Fearing He 'May Not Return Alive'
stories.summary:
Pakistan's jailed former prime minister Imran Khan has appealed for urgent medical treatment, saying his and his wife's health are deteriorating. In a letter published by his lawyer Salman Safdar, the 74-year-old wrote that "this unrelenting state is taking me to a place from which I may not return alive." He said doctors have told him he is highly vulnerable to brain haemorrhage and cardiac arrest, and that his heart has already suffered damage.

Khan said he is held in solitary confinement for up to 22 hours a day, without family visits, books or television, and has seen his lawyers only four times in the past year. He also said his wife, Bushra Bibi, suffered a detached retina in April and may lose her sight without further surgery. His family previously said he lost most of the vision in his right eye.

The government disputes the claims. Parliamentary affairs minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry said Khan is "the most well-accommodated prisoner in Pakistan," and authorities say doctors see him weekly and assess his health as satisfactory. Officials say he was taken to a government hospital for an eye injection a week ago and was deemed clinically stable.

Khan, who has been jailed since August 2023 and faces more than 100 charges that he calls politically motivated, remains influential. Thousands of his supporters marched in early October demanding his release, after which authorities imposed a crackdown and a state of emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
